sources.title: Stewart KM (2001) The commercial bark harvest of the African cherry (Prunus africana) on Mount Oku, Cameroon (PhD thesis); matrices as archived in COMPADRE
sources.summary: One unharvested plot vs four harvested plots (once or twice per year), 1997-1999. No DOI; single control plot means the contrast has no replication on the control side. The thesis abstract reports lambda below 1 in harvested plots; 6 of 8 single-year harvested matrices here are below 1, but the 1997-99 mean matrices used for this comparison are at or above 1 in 3 of 4 plots. A later forest-wide harvest (2005/06) is outside these matrices (Stewart 2009, For Ecol Manage 258:1121).

cards.issue: Evidence from another species harvested for bark: Garcinia lucida
cards.why_it_matters: Long-term growth rate by scenario (No bark harvest: λ 1.063; Partial debarking (one side): λ 1.060; Ring-barking (whole circumference): λ 1.057; Felling at 1 m after fruiting: λ 1.057; Felling at 1 m before fruiting: λ 1.056). λ below 1 means a population that shrinks if conditions persist.
cards.uncertainty: Different species and site: life history and recovery may differ; treat as a warning sign, not a number for this plant.
cards.recommended_next: Look for a study on this species; until then monitor plots before and after harvest.

sources.title: Guedje NM, Zuidema PA, During H, Foahom B, Lejoly J (2007) Tree bark as a non-timber forest product [Garcinia lucida]. For Ecol Manage 240:1-12
sources.summary: Growth rate hides the damage here: the authors find the stock of harvestable trees falls to about half in 20 years under annual partial debarking and below 4% under annual ring-barking or felling, although lambda stays near 1. EthnoHarvest does not compute the harvestable stock. Matrix models for three local practices, built from a two-year field study (1997-1999); felling matrices have 9 stages, the others 8, so no LTRE is shown for felling.
